shinyasync is deployment-agnostic: an app that runs locally runs the same way
on Shiny Server, Posit Connect, a container or behind a multi-process load
balancer. What changes between them is how many workers each R process should
have.

## Sizing the pool

Each R process gets its own daemon pool. Unless you call `pool_async()`, the
first task starts one with one less worker than the cores available to the
process; a container's CPU quota or cpuset counts, as on Posit Connect. To set
the size yourself, call it at the top level of `app.R`, so the pool is started
once per process and held until the app stops:

```{r}
library(shiny)
library(shinyasync)

pool_async(workers = 4)

ui <- fluidPage(...)
server <- function(input, output, session) { ... }
shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Under a multi-process load balancer such as
[faucet](https://github.com/ixpantia/faucet) or Posit Connect with several
processes per app, every process starts its own pool. Size `workers` so that
`processes × workers` fits the host, or point every process at one shared
remote daemon set. The arguments of `pool_async()` pass through to
`mirai::daemons()`:

```{r}
pool_async(url = "tcp://daemon-host:5555")
```

If you already manage `mirai::daemons()` yourself, skip `pool_async()`; the
package uses the daemons you set and leaves them alone.

## Monitoring the pool

Tasks run first come, first served across one pool, so a button-triggered task
can wait behind background refreshes. `mirai::status()` reports the worker
count, how many tasks are executing and how many are waiting for a worker, so a
task monitor can show why something has not started:

```{r}
output$pool <- renderText({
  invalidateLater(1000)
  s <- mirai::status()
  sprintf("%d workers, %d running, %d queued",
          s$connections, s$mirai[["executing"]], s$mirai[["awaiting"]])
})
```

Each worker attaches a package the first time a task needs it; later tasks on
that worker find it already attached.

## Preloading the workers

Objects a task refers to are serialized to the worker on every run, and a
database connection cannot be serialized at all. Run the code that creates them
once on every worker instead:

```{r}
pool_async(workers = 4, everywhere = {
  sales <- arrow::read_parquet("data/sales.parquet")  # one copy per worker
  con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "app.db")  # cannot be serialized
  rates <- fx_rates                                   # shipped once from the session
  .Last <- function() DBI::dbDisconnect(con)          # runs when the worker exits
})

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  by_region <- reactiveAsync(summarise_sales(sales, con, input$region))
}
```

The expression runs with `mirai::everywhere()` when the pool starts, before any
task. Objects it refers to are resolved in the calling environment and sent
once; the names it assigns and those objects are *resident*, so tasks do not
ship them even when the session holds an object of the same name, and
`print()` shows them on a `resident` line.

Things to know before relying on it:

- **Call it at the top level of `app.R`**, so the preload runs once per
  process and connections live until the app stops.
- **Resident data is static.** Data that changes belongs in a reactive read.
- **Every worker holds its own copy and opens its own connection**, so size
  memory and the database's connection limit by `processes × workers`.
- **Close connections with `.Last`.** Assign a `.Last` function in the
  expression: R runs it when the worker process exits, on pool shutdown and
  when the app process dies, and the pool does not wait for it.
- **Late daemons are not preloaded.** A daemon that joins after the preload,
  as a remote daemon may, does not receive it; a task using a resident name
  there fails with a message saying so.
